q: Fill up: In pregnancy total T4 rises because oestrogen increases ______, so the best screening test of thyroid function is ______.
opts: thyroxine-binding globulin; TSH
TSH; total T4
albumin; total T3
hCG; a TRH stimulation test
exp: Oestrogen raises TBG and hence total T4, which is why free T4 and TSH rather than total T4 are used to judge thyroid status in pregnancy.

q: A 28-year-old at 12 weeks with known Graves disease presents with fever of 39 C, a pulse of 150/min, profuse vomiting and new atrial fibrillation. What is the diagnosis and the first drug?
opts: Thyroid storm — start propylthiouracil, then iodine an hour later, with a beta blocker
Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis — reassure and repeat the thyroid profile in 4 weeks
Graves disease in pregnancy — start methimazole and plan radioiodine ablation after delivery now
Thyroid storm — start carbimazole and proceed to immediate delivery of the fetus
exp: Thyroid storm is a medical emergency: propylthiouracil blocks both synthesis and T4-to-T3 conversion, iodine is given after an hour, and beta blockade controls the rate.

q: Which of the following statements about placental transfer in diabetic pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: Glucose crosses the placenta by facilitated diffusion but insulin does not, so the fetal pancreas makes its own insulin
Maternal insulin crosses the placenta freely and is the main driver of fetal macrosomia
Neither glucose nor insulin crosses the placenta, so the fetus depends on amino acids and lactate alone
Anti-TSH receptor antibodies cross the placenta, but neither glucose nor insulin can cross it
exp: Maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia because glucose crosses freely while insulin, and most oral agents such as glyburide, cross poorly.

q: Fill up: Universal screening for gestational diabetes is performed at ______ weeks, and women with strong risk factors are additionally tested ______.
opts: 24-28; at the first antenatal visit
24-28; only at 34 weeks
11-14; at 24 weeks
32-34; at the first visit
exp: All women are screened at 24-28 weeks, and those with risk factors are screened early at booking and retested later if the first test is normal.

q: All of the following are part of postpartum follow-up after gestational diabetes EXCEPT:
opts: Discharging her from follow-up once a single normal test is obtained at six weeks
A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 6-12 weeks postpartum
Lifelong screening for diabetes every one to three years
Contraception and preconception counselling before the next pregnancy
exp: Gestational diabetes marks a lifelong risk of type 2 diabetes, so surveillance every 1-3 years continues after the 6-12 week test.

q: Match the timing of poor diabetic control with its fetal consequence — 1) Periconception with HbA1c above 10% 2) Hyperglycaemia during organogenesis 3) Hyperglycaemia in the third trimester … A) Caudal regression, cardiac and renal anomalies B) Spontaneous abortion and major malformation C) Macrosomia, polyhydramnios and neonatal hypoglycaemia
exp: Teratogenic damage happens in organogenesis and scales with HbA1c, whereas late hyperglycaemia drives fetal overgrowth and organomegaly.

q: Fill up: Women with pregestational diabetes are advised ______ mg of folic acid daily, because their pregnancies carry a higher risk of ______.
opts: 5; neural tube defects
0.4; cardiac anomalies
5; renal agenesis
0.4; skeletal dysplasia
exp: High-dose folic acid (4-5 mg) preconceptionally reduces the excess of neural tube defects seen in diabetic embryopathy.

q: Which of the following statements about antenatal surveillance in pregestational diabetes is TRUE?
opts: Serial growth scans and antepartum testing from 32-34 weeks are standard when control is poor or vasculopathy is present
Fetal karyotyping is mandatory because maternal diabetes raises the risk of fetal trisomy 21
Amniocentesis for lung maturity is required before every diabetic delivery, whatever the gestation
Serum alpha-fetoprotein screening is unreliable in diabetes and must never be offered
exp: Surveillance intensity matches disease severity; diabetes does not raise aneuploidy risk, and AFP screening is still offered for neural tube defects.

q: A 32-year-old with type 1 diabetes at 10 weeks records fasting glucose of 130 mg/dL and two-hour postprandial values of 190 mg/dL on a twice-daily premixed insulin. What is the next step?
opts: Change to a basal-bolus regimen of short-acting and intermediate insulin and titrate to targets
Stop insulin and switch to metformin, since injected insulin is teratogenic in the first trimester
Add bedtime glyburide and continue the present insulin doses unchanged
Take no action, because glycaemic targets only matter in the third trimester
exp: Insulin is the drug of choice in pregestational diabetes; a basal-bolus regimen with titration to fasting and postprandial targets is needed.

q: Fill up: In well-controlled gestational diabetes without complications, delivery is planned around ______ weeks, while poorly controlled diabetes with vasculopathy is delivered by ______ weeks.
exp: Uncomplicated well-controlled gestational diabetes is delivered at term, but vasculopathy or poor control shifts delivery earlier after documenting lung maturity.

q: Fill up: The DIPSI test uses ______ g of glucose regardless of the fasting state, and gestational diabetes is diagnosed when the two-hour value is ______ mg/dL or higher.
exp: DIPSI is a single-step non-fasting 75 g test with a single two-hour cut-off of 140 mg/dL, which is why it suits busy antenatal clinics.

q: A 30-year-old at 28 weeks is diagnosed with gestational diabetes (DIPSI two-hour value 165 mg/dL). After two weeks of medical nutrition therapy her fasting glucose is 98 mg/dL and her two-hour postprandial value is 130 mg/dL. What is the next step?
opts: Start insulin, or metformin if she declines insulin, while continuing nutrition therapy and glucose monitoring
Deliver the baby now, because medical nutrition therapy has failed
Add an oral hypoglycaemic agent only if targets remain uncontrolled after 36 weeks
Reassure her, because both readings are at target and no treatment is needed
exp: Persistent fasting values above 95 mg/dL or postprandial values above 120 mg/dL despite two weeks of nutrition therapy call for pharmacotherapy.

q: Fill up: The usual glycaemic targets in pregnancy are a fasting glucose below ______ mg/dL and a two-hour postprandial glucose below ______ mg/dL.
exp: Typical targets are fasting below 95 mg/dL, one-hour postprandial below 140 mg/dL and two-hour postprandial below 120 mg/dL.

q: Which of the following statements about medical nutrition therapy in gestational diabetes is TRUE?
opts: Energy is spread over three small meals and two or three snacks, with about 40-50% coming from low-glycaemic carbohydrate
Severe restriction to 1200 kcal a day improves outcomes by preventing fetal macrosomia
Avoiding carbohydrate altogether is the quickest way to reach glycaemic targets
Weight loss of about 1 kg a week is recommended for every woman with gestational diabetes
exp: Ketosis from severe calorie or carbohydrate restriction is harmful; modest energy intake with distributed low-glycaemic carbohydrate is the goal.

q: All of the following statements about metformin in gestational diabetes are true EXCEPT:
opts: It is contraindicated in pregnancy because it causes severe fetal hypoglycaemia
It crosses the placenta freely, so the fetus is exposed to it
It is an option for women who refuse or cannot use insulin
Long-term offspring follow-up is reassuring but data remain incomplete
exp: Metformin crosses the placenta and is used where insulin is refused or impractical; neonatal hypoglycaemia is far commoner with glyburide than metformin.

q: Fill up: The usual starting total daily insulin dose in pregnancy is about ______ units per kg body weight, of which roughly ______ is given as basal insulin.
exp: Total daily insulin starts at 0.7-1.0 units/kg, split so that about half is basal and half covers meals, then titrated to self-monitored glucose.

q: A woman with insulin-treated gestational diabetes presents in early labour at 39 weeks with a capillary glucose of 88 mg/dL. What is the intrapartum plan?
opts: Stop subcutaneous insulin, run a variable-rate insulin and dextrose infusion targeting 70-110 mg/dL, and stop it after delivery
Continue her usual subcutaneous insulin doses unchanged throughout labour
Give no insulin during labour and check the glucose only after delivery
Stop insulin and infuse 5% dextrose alone, without any glucose monitoring
exp: Labour needs a sliding-scale insulin-dextrose infusion to keep glucose between 70 and 110 mg/dL, and requirements fall sharply once the placenta is delivered.

q: Fill up: After delivery, insulin requirements in pregestational diabetes ______, and the postpartum dose is usually about ______ of the late-pregnancy dose.
opts: fall sharply; half or less
rise sharply; double
stay the same; the full dose
fall sharply; twice
exp: Loss of the placental hormones that cause insulin resistance means requirements plummet after delivery, often to half or less of the antenatal dose.

q: All of the following are maternal complications of diabetes in pregnancy EXCEPT:
opts: Placenta previa
Pre-eclampsia
Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis
Polyhydramnios
exp: Pre-eclampsia, candidiasis, polyhydramnios, infections and progression of retinopathy and nephropathy are all linked to diabetes; placenta previa is not.

q: Match the mechanism with its consequence — 1) Pedersen hypothesis 2) Diabetic embryopathy in the first trimester 3) Neonatal hypoglycaemia after cord clamping … A) Caudal regression and cardiac anomalies B) Fetal hyperinsulinaemia causing macrosomia and organomegaly C) Continued fetal insulin action once the maternal glucose supply stops
exp: Maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia (Pedersen), early hyperglycaemia malforms the embryo, and sustained fetal insulin causes postnatal hypoglycaemia.

q: Which of the following statements about the infant of a diabetic mother is TRUE?
opts: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia antagonises cortisol and delays surfactant maturation, raising the risk of respiratory distress at any gestation
Neonatal hypoglycaemia is rare, because the fetal pancreas involutes promptly after delivery
Neonatal polycythaemia and jaundice result from fetal hypo-insulinaemia and reduced oxygen consumption
Amniocentesis to document lung maturity is mandatory before every delivery in a diabetic pregnancy
exp: Hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant, chronic intrauterine hyperglycaemia drives polycythaemia, and lung maturity testing is selective, not universal.

q: Fill up: Phosphatidylglycerol appears in amniotic fluid at about ______ weeks, and its presence is taken to indicate ______.
opts: 35; fetal lung maturity
28; fetal lung maturity
35; fetal anaemia
32; meconium-stained liquor
exp: A lecithin-sphingomyelin ratio of 2:1 and the appearance of phosphatidylglycerol around 35 weeks both indicate that the fetal lungs are mature.

q: Fill up: The first manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia is ______, which works by ______.
opts: McRoberts positioning; flattening the lumbar lordosis and rotating the symphysis pubis upwards
fundal pressure; driving the anterior shoulder below the symphysis pubis
the Zavanelli manoeuvre; replacing the head before caesarean delivery
the Woods corkscrew; widening the bisacromial diameter of the shoulders
exp: Hyperflexing the maternal thighs on the abdomen flattens the sacral promontory and rotates the symphysis, freeing the impacted anterior shoulder.

q: McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure have failed and the anterior shoulder is still impacted behind the symphysis. Which manoeuvre should be attempted next?
opts: Internal rotation with Woods corkscrew or Rubin II, or delivery of the posterior arm
Fundal pressure applied by an assistant while traction continues
Immediate Zavanelli manoeuvre and caesarean delivery
Symphysiotomy before any rotational manoeuvre is attempted
exp: After McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, internal rotation or posterior arm delivery reduces the bisacromial diameter; fundal pressure is contraindicated.

q: All of the following are recognised fetal complications of shoulder dystocia EXCEPT:
opts: Congenital talipes equinovarus
Erb's palsy and Klumpke's palsy
Fracture of the clavicle or humerus
Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy from delayed delivery
exp: Brachial plexus injury, long-bone fracture and asphyxia follow traumatic delivery and prolonged head-to-body interval; talipes is not caused by shoulder dystocia.
